weather: acid drizzle beading on every surface
a hard rain that turns the streetlights into smeared bars of colour
fog thick enough to swallow the block across the street
unseasonal heat, the asphalt breathing it back up after dark
sleet, sideways, finding every gap in a lined coat
a dry electric wind off the Sound that makes the drones drift
the flat grey light of a sky that has not cleared in nine days
a break in the clouds, and for once you can see stars over the sprawl
sound: bass from three floors down, felt in the teeth rather than heard
the arrhythmic clatter of a maglev overhead
an advertising drone repeating the same jingle in four languages
the wet mechanical cough of a failing air scrubber
someone arguing in Salish through a thin wall
the hum of a badly shielded transformer
silence, which in this neighbourhood is worse than noise
smell: soykaf, cigarette smoke, and something under it that is not food
ozone from a fresh magical discharge
industrial solvent and cheap incense competing badly
the iron smell of the Sound at low tide
sweat, gun oil, and the antiseptic tang of a clinic
frying nutrisoy from a cart that has not moved in a decade
detail: an AR tag someone has bothered to render in three dimensions
a shrine of cheap candles under a bullet-pocked wall
a Lone Star drone parked and powered down, gathering rust
graffiti that updates itself when you look away
a child's bicycle chained to a pipe, both long abandoned
a corp logo half-scraped off a door that still locks
a queue of people who have clearly been waiting all night
a dead pigeon with a datajack in the back of its skull
a vending machine that only accepts a currency that stopped existing
crowd: shift workers spilling out of a plant, too tired to look up
a gang tagging territory with unhurried confidence
tourists who took a wrong turn and know it
a street preacher warning about the next Awakening
nobody at all, which is itself information
day labourers waiting for a truck that may not come
a knot of teenagers running BTL chips off a cracked commlink
corp security on their break, armour half-unfastened
cold_open: The call comes in at the worst possible hour, which is how you know it pays.
You have been in the car for forty minutes and nobody has said anything.
It starts, as these things do, with a name you were hoping never to hear again.
The meet is already going wrong and it has not started yet.
Someone has left the door open. Nobody in this business leaves a door open.
There is blood on the floor and it is not yours yet.
Three hours ago this was a simple job. Two hours ago it stopped being one.
